analysis.one_liner: Requires new large carbon dioxide emitters to buy offsets, creating a market for emission reductions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in June 1991 with 15 cosponsors, it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to require any new large carbon dioxide source — power plants, factories, and other facilities emitting 100,000 tons a year or more — to obtain a permit and buy certified CO2 offset credits covering its emissions [S2][S3]. Credits could be earned by fuel-switching, planting and preserving forests, more efficient cars and appliances, capturing methane from landfills and coalbeds, cogeneration, and renewable energy replacing fossil units [S2][S3]. Sources that emitted more than they offset would pay a $250-per-ton penalty, adjusted for inflation, and offset the excess the next year [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and, three months later, to its Energy and Power subcommittee; neither ever acted on it [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be the public through reduced greenhouse gas emissions and reduced oil dependence, since new fossil-fuel plants would have had to pay for their carbon or switch to cleaner fuels [S2][S3]. New revenue streams would also have opened for forest landowners, renewable energy developers, cogeneration operators, makers of efficient vehicles and appliances, and methane-capture projects, all of whom could sell certified offset credits [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public; forestry, renewable, and efficiency businesses

how_it_helps.text: New major CO2 sources could not operate without a permit requiring certified offset credits equal to their emissions, so each new large emitter would have had to pay for reductions elsewhere — the first federal mechanism putting a price on new carbon emissions [S2][S3].

The bill allowed continued use of coal, the most abundant domestic fuel, while making emitters internalize the climate cost, which its findings argued would spur efficiency, cut the trade deficit, and reduce dependence on foreign oil [S3].

Credit eligibility covered a wide range of real reductions — fuel switching under the Clean Air Act's acid rain title, new forests under 100-year easements, vehicle and appliance efficiency beyond 1990 levels, methane capture, cogeneration, utility repowering, and renewables replacing identifiable fossil units — with EPA certification rules and a public National CO2 Offset Bank to track and retire credits [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of new large CO2 sources — chiefly electric utilities and industrial facilities building or expanding fossil-fueled plants — would bear the cost of permits, offset credits, and any $250-per-ton excess emissions penalties, and those costs would largely flow to their customers through energy prices [S2][S3]. Federal and state agencies would also bear the administrative cost of certifying credits and running permit programs [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: New fossil-fuel plants and their customers

drawbacks.text: The offset requirement applied only to new major sources, not existing ones, so total U.S. emissions would have kept rising as long as new plants paid for offsets rather than avoided emissions — a cost passed to consumers through energy prices [S3].

The scheme depended on EPA certifying hard-to-measure reductions, such as per-acre carbon fixation by tree species over 100 years and appliance efficiency estimated over expected lifetimes; badly set baselines or easements could yield credits that did not reflect real emission cuts [S3].
The $250-per-ton excess emissions penalty, adjusted annually for inflation, would be an added cost for any new plant that miscalculated its credit purchases [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was an early, market-based attempt to price carbon for new emitters while explicitly preserving coal use, which made it a modest instrument: it covered only new sources and relied on offset certification that could be gamed if EPA's baselines were weak. Its costs would have shown up in energy prices for new plants, but its backers argued efficiency incentives would partly offset that. Its main flaw was scope, not design — it was a small first step, and it never got even a subcommittee vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, then to its Energy and Power subcommittee in September 1991, and no markup, hearing vote, or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Cooper (D-TN) introduced the bill on June 18, 1991, joined by Reps. Synar, Studds, Markey, and Boehlert, and it drew 15 cosponsors — 12 Democrats and 3 Republicans [S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction [S1][S5].

On September 9, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, where the record ends; the bill never received a hearing-reported action, markup, or vote in the House or Senate before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Entities planning new large fossil-fuel sources — chiefly electric utilities and industrial emitters — were better off, since no federal offset requirement or carbon penalty ever took effect from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 12 Democrats and 3 Republicans — but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where the parties actually stood.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and other new large fossil-fuel emitters
industries.note: New plants emitting 100,000+ tons of CO2 a year would have needed permits, offset credits, and faced a $250-per-ton penalty for excess emissions. Their interest in defeating the bill was avoiding those compliance costs, which would otherwise have been passed to customers.

The bill let landowners sell certified credits for new forests, improved management, and old-growth preservation, but only under recorded easements barring harvest for 100 years. Land with high timber value would have been locked out of harvesting while earning credit revenue instead.

Renewables replacing identifiable fossil utility sources, and cogeneration replacing industrial boilers, could sell certified CO2 credits, creating a new revenue stream that made clean energy more competitive.

The bill's findings framed offsets as a way to keep using coal, but credits were also earned by fuel-switching away from coal and by utility repowering, so coal demand at new plants would have faced a carbon price.

Manufacturers could sell credits for efficiency improvements beyond their 1990 sales performance, but no credits were allowed for efficiency already required by federal law, limiting the payoff to genuinely voluntary gains.
